title: Backpropagation on a tape
starter:
def grads(tape: list) -> list[float]:
    """tape[i] is ('x', v), ('const', v), ('add', a, b) or ('mul', a, b), where a and b index
    earlier entries. Return d(last entry)/d(entry i) for every i."""
    g = [0.0] * len(tape)
    g[-1] = 1.0                                        # the seed: d(last)/d(last) = 1
    return g
hints: Two passes. Forward: compute each entry's value in order. Backward: from the last entry to the first.
An add passes its gradient to both operands unchanged. A mul passes g · (the other operand's value) to each side.
Use +=, never =: an entry used twice (like ('mul', 0, 0)) receives two contributions, and the derivative is their sum.
prompt: A tape is a program as a list: entry i is ('x', v) (an input), ('const', v), ('add', a, b) or ('mul', a, b), where a and b are earlier entries. Write grads(tape): the derivative of the last entry with respect to every entry, as a list. Compute every value forward, seed the last entry with 1.0, then walk backward and send each entry's gradient to its operands.

answer.code:
def grads(tape: list) -> list[float]:
    """tape[i] is ('x', v), ('const', v), ('add', a, b) or ('mul', a, b), where a and b index
    earlier entries. Return d(last entry)/d(entry i) for every i."""
    vals = []
    for node in tape:                                  # forward: every value, in order
        op = node[0]
        if op in ('x', 'const'):
            vals.append(node[1])
        elif op == 'add':
            vals.append(vals[node[1]] + vals[node[2]])
        else:
            vals.append(vals[node[1]] * vals[node[2]])
    g = [0.0] * len(tape)
    g[-1] = 1.0                                        # the seed
    for i in range(len(tape) - 1, -1, -1):             # backward: each node passes its gradient down
        op = tape[i][0]
        if op == 'add':
            g[tape[i][1]] += g[i]
            g[tape[i][2]] += g[i]
        elif op == 'mul':
            a, b = tape[i][1], tape[i][2]
            g[a] += g[i] * vals[b]
            g[b] += g[i] * vals[a]
    return g
answer.explain: This is reverse mode in miniature. Walking the tape backward guarantees every entry has received all its contributions before it passes its own gradient on, because users always come later on the tape than what they use. x · x at 3 gives 6: two contributions of 3 each. The += is the whole trick, and it's why the spec has to say in which order the contributions are added: in f32, the order changes the bits.
